title: Countersign
pitch: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log.
about_excerpt: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent highlights the quantity cell on the scan after the match flags line 1: 120 invoiced, 100 received. Agent recommends HOLD. Approve stays disabled until the issue is resolved. The tool call waits for this click. Two-phase countersign: click, 25 s timeout, or abort. Timeout returns pending. Only the human click can approve. 4 queue tools always on, 9 invoice tools while an invoice is open, back to 4 on close. Blue reads, amber writes. Client-only: one registerTool path, Chrome budgets enforced, Zod schemas, clamped JSON, every call audited. One review, hop by hop: tool call → wrapper → domain → UI → request_countersign waits → human click → resolver → agent. One audit log for both sides: agent calls in blue, reviewer clicks in green, with arguments, result, duration. Tools tab: 13 tools, live state, call counts, last input and output, copyable example input for Chrome inspector. Agent comments pinned to a field; the reviewer replies; the agent reads the reply on its next tool call. LF-2026-0942: line 3 not on the PO and its text tells the agent to approve. Match catches it; click still rules. Ten synthetic invoices, one planted fact each, generated deterministically with draw-time bounding boxes. Chrome DevTools > Application > WebMCP: 13 tools registered by the page, 18 calls counted, 0 failed. Inspiration Accounts-payable teams review thousands of invoices a month. The work splits cleanly in two: matching numbers against a purchase order and a goods receipt, which an agent does perfectly and a human hates, and looking at the scanned page to see whether the number the agent read is really the number printed there, which a human does in two seconds and an agent cannot do at all. Today the two halves live in different tools, and an agent that approves a duplicate is a segregation-of-duties failure with a dollar sign on it. Every WebMCP showcase app I found was consumer or commerce: pizza, flights, greeting cards. None had money at stake, a mandatory human sign-off, or an audit trail. Countersign is the control: the agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record. What it does Countersign is an invoice-review workbench with thirteen WebMCP tools registered in the page. In the ChatGPT desktop browser (or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) you say "Work through my review queue" and the agent: lists the queue and opens an invoice on your screen; runs a three-way match against the PO and the goods receipt, line by line, with the vendor's price tolerance and tax arithmetic; searches every other invoice for duplicates ( INV-2291 and 2291 normalize to the same number); checks the vendor profile, including the bank account printed on the document against the one on file; draws a highlight on the scanned page for every number it cites, so you verify it where it is printed; flags typed, severity-rated issues; proposes GL codes for invoices with no PO; posts comments you can reply to; requests your countersign . A card slides in with its recommendation. The tool call waits up to 25 seconds for your click. Only your click can approve. Every tool call and every human click lands in one audit log. Ten synthetic invoices ship with the demo, each with one planted fact: a quantity overbill, a price above tolerance, a duplicate of an approved invoice, a changed bank account under a stamp, a missing PO, a two-cent tax rounding error, and one whose line description tries to instruct the agent to approve it. Live: https://countersign-theta.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/rushabhT3/countersign Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Structured extraction — amounts, quantities, invoice numbers, confidence scores — is exactly the data an agent should receive by tool call, not by reading pixels. A scanned invoice table is the worst possible actuation target on the web: dense, tabular, low contrast, and often stamped over. Countersign exposes the extraction and the matching logic as typed tools with JSON Schemas, and it exposes them in the reviewer's page , where the same call that returns a value can also draw the evidence on screen. The tools are state-scoped. Four queue tools are registered for the life of the page. Nine invoice tools appear only while an invoice is open and are unregistered when the workbench returns to empty, so the agent works on the same document the human is looking at and cannot check invoice A while the reviewer looks at B. That is a WebMCP-native idea: the page's UI state is the agent's context. How it creates a better user experience The reviewer never re-types or re-computes. The agent never touches money without a click. Evidence appears where the reviewer is already looking: show_field_evidence draws the highlight on the page image and the Match tab fills in as the agent works. Activity toasts show every call as it happens. The countersign card shows how long the agent has been waiting for the click, highlights an issue's evidence when you hover it, and takes A / H / R / Esc. If the reviewer types a reply in the Comments tab, the agent reads it on its next call. A Tools tab inside the product shows all thirteen tools with live state, call counts, last input and output, and a ready-to-paste example input for anyone driving the tools by hand. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A remote MCP server can read the same data, but it cannot draw a box on the reviewer's screen, cannot open a card inside their signed-in session, and cannot make its own call block on their click on the same page. With WebMCP the agent and the reviewer share one document, one state, and one audit log. The agent does the forty-line match; the human does the two-second visual check and the decision; the log shows who did what, with arguments and timing. How we built it Imperative WebMCP API only , registered from a client component in the top-level page. One document.modelContext.registerTool(definition, { signal }) call site in lib/webmcp/registry.ts , with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome 149. Zod 4 schemas as the single source of truth : z.toJSONSchema produces the advertised schema, safeParse validates every call, and the wrapper turns errors into sentences that name the recovery step ("Call list_invoices to see valid ids."). Chrome's budgets enforced in code : defineTool throws in development if a name exceeds 30 characters, a description 500, or a parameter description 150; every output is clamped to 1,500 characters and stays valid JSON. Annotations carry readOnlyHint on reads and untrustedContentHint on anything that returns document text. Two-phase countersign : request_countersign creates a pending decision and races the reviewer's click, a 25-second timeout, and the AbortSignal. On timeout it returns

live_observation.first_impression: A queue of invoice records is shown with amounts, vendors, and review/approved statuses; invoice detail tabs are initially disabled. The workflow is recognizable as human invoice review.
live_observation.action_attempted: Opened invoice INV-10231 from the review queue.
live_observation.after_state: An Invoice page opened with Fields selected, extracted values and confidence percentages, plus Run match, Find duplicates, Flag issue, Comment, and Request decision actions.
live_observation.notes: The detail view exposes audit-oriented controls and field-level Show buttons; no approval was attempted.
